title: Edit Operations & Edit Scripts: Insertion, Deletion, Substitution
h1: Edit Operations & Edit Scripts: Insertion, Deletion, Substitution
primary_entity_candidate: Edit Operations & Edit Scripts: Insertion, Deletion, Substitution

sections.heading: Edit Operations & Edit Scripts: Insertion, Deletion, Substitution
sections.evidence: Edit operations are elementary transformations used to describe how one sequence can be changed into another.
paragraphs: Edit operations are elementary transformations used to describe how one sequence can be changed into another.
In standard Levenshtein distance, the permitted edit operations are:
insertion,
deletion,
substitution.
An edit script is an ordered sequence of these operations. The minimum cost of any valid script transforming the source sequence into the target sequence defines the Levenshtein distance.
source sequence ↓ edit operations ↓ target sequence minimum valid script cost = Levenshtein distance

The operation model becomes meaningful only after the sequence representation has been defined. One edit can act on bytes, Unicode code points, grapheme clusters, words, phonemes, biological symbols, or another application-defined unit.

sections.heading: What Is an Edit Operation?
sections.evidence: Let Σ be an alphabet and Σ* the set of finite sequences over that alphabet.
paragraphs: Let Σ be an alphabet and Σ* the set of finite sequences over that alphabet.
An edit operation makes a local change to a sequence.
Operation Effect Example Standard Cost Insertion Add one sequence element ct → cat 1 Deletion Remove one sequence element cart → cat 1 Substitution Replace one sequence element cat → cut 1
A match is often represented in an alignment, but it is not normally counted as an edit because it does not change the sequence.
match(a,a) cost = 0 insert(a) cost = 1 delete(a) cost = 1 substitute(a,b) cost = 1

sections.heading: Insertion
sections.evidence: An insertion adds one sequence element.
paragraphs: An insertion adds one sequence element.
ct ↓ insert a cat
At the chosen representation level, insertion increases sequence length by one.
If the sequence elements are words rather than characters:
[the, cat] ↓ insert "black" [the, black, cat]
the same abstract operation applies to a different kind of sequence.

sections.heading: Deletion
sections.evidence: A deletion removes one sequence element.
paragraphs: A deletion removes one sequence element.
cart ↓ delete r cat
Deletion decreases sequence length by one element at the selected representation layer.

sections.heading: Substitution
sections.evidence: A substitution replaces one sequence element with another.
paragraphs: A substitution replaces one sequence element with another.
cat ↓ substitute a → u cut
A substitution preserves sequence length.
Under standard unit-cost Levenshtein distance:
substitution cost = 1
but generalized edit-distance models can assign another cost.

sections.heading: Transformation Direction Matters
sections.evidence: Edit operations are interpreted relative to a transformation direction:
paragraphs: Edit operations are interpreted relative to a transformation direction:
source → target
Consider:
cat → cart
From source to target, the change is an insertion of r .
Reversing the direction:
cart → cat
changes the corresponding operation to deletion.
Forward Operation Reverse Operation Insert a Delete a Delete a Insert a Substitute a → b Substitute b → a
With symmetric unit costs, reversing an optimal script produces a reverse transformation with the same total cost. This contributes to the symmetry of standard Levenshtein distance.

sections.heading: What Is an Edit Script?
sections.evidence: An edit script is an ordered sequence of permitted edit operations that transforms the source into the target.
paragraphs: An edit script is an ordered sequence of permitted edit operations that transforms the source into the target.
Applying those operations sequentially gives:
x ↓ o1 x1 ↓ o2 x2 ... ↓ ok y
A script is valid only if applying all of its operations produces the exact target sequence.

sections.heading: Example: Kitten to Sitting
sections.evidence: kitten ↓ substitute k → s sitten ↓ substitute e → i sittin ↓ insert g sitting
paragraphs: kitten ↓ substitute k → s sitten ↓ substitute e → i sittin ↓ insert g sitting
This script contains two substitutions and one insertion.
total cost = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3
Under standard unit-cost Levenshtein distance:
ED("kitten", "sitting") = 3

sections.heading: Edit Script Cost
sections.evidence: Let c(o) denote the cost of operation o .
paragraphs: Let c(o) denote the cost of operation o .
The cost of an edit script S is:
C(S) = Σ c(oi)
Standard Levenshtein distance uses:
c(insert) = 1 c(delete) = 1 c(substitute) = 1
The distance is the minimum script cost:
d(x,y) = min C(S) over every valid script S such that S(x) = y
Therefore:
edit distance ≠ cost of any valid edit script edit distance = cost of a minimum-cost valid edit script

sections.heading: A Valid Script Is Not Necessarily Optimal
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
cat → cut
One valid script is:
cat ↓ delete a ct ↓ insert u cut
Its total cost is two.
A cheaper script is:
cat ↓ substitute a → u cut
whose cost is one.
Both scripts are valid. Only the second is optimal under the standard unit-cost model.

sections.heading: Substitution Versus Delete Plus Insert
sections.evidence: A substitution can always be represented as a deletion followed by an insertion.
paragraphs: A substitution can always be represented as a deletion followed by an insertion.
uav ↓ delete a uv ↓ insert b ubv
Under the standard cost model:
substitution = 1 deletion + insertion = 2
so direct substitution is cheaper.
In a weighted model, if:
c_substitute(a,b) ≥ c_delete(a) + c_insert(b)
then using substitution provides no cost advantage over deleting a and inserting b .
See Weighted Levenshtein Distance .

sections.heading: Edit Scripts and Alignments
sections.evidence: An edit script can also be represented as an alignment.
paragraphs: An edit script can also be represented as an alignment.
source: c a t | * | target: c u t
Here:
| = match * = substitution
An insertion can be shown as a gap in the source:
source: c - t target: c a t
A deletion can be shown as a gap in the target:
source: c a t target: c - t
Alignment Column Interpretation a / a Match a / b Substitution - / b Insertion a / - Deletion

sections.heading: Edit Operations in Dynamic Programming
sections.evidence: The Wagner–Fischer Algorithm computes the minimum cost of transforming prefixes of one sequence into prefixes of another.
paragraphs: The Wagner–Fischer Algorithm computes the minimum cost of transforming prefixes of one sequence into prefixes of another.
Define:
D[i][j]
as the minimum cost required to transform the first i source elements into the first j target elements.
Under standard unit costs:
D[i][j] = min( D[i-1][j] + 1, D[i][j-1] + 1, D[i-1][j-1] + cost ) cost = 0 if source[i-1] == target[j-1] 1 otherwise
Transition Meaning D[i-1][j] → D[i][j] Deletion D[i][j-1] → D[i][j] Insertion D[i-1][j-1] → D[i][j] with unequal elements Substitution D[i-1][j-1] → D[i][j] with equal elements Match

The visual direction of a matrix transition depends on which sequence is placed on each axis. The semantic operation should therefore be determined from the prefix-state definition rather than memorized from a particular diagram orientation.

sections.heading: An Edit Script Is a Path Through Prefix States
sections.evidence: A complete edit script corresponds to a path from:
paragraphs: A complete edit script corresponds to a path from:
to:
(m,n)
in the dynamic-programming state space.
Operation Source Elements Consumed Target Elements Consumed Deletion 1 0 Insertion 0 1 Substitution 1 1 Match 1 1

sections.heading: Recovering an Edit Script
sections.evidence: Once a complete dynamic-programming matrix has been computed, an optimal edit script can be recovered by backtracking from the final state.
paragraphs: Once a complete dynamic-programming matrix has been computed, an optimal edit script can be recovered by backtracking from the final state.

i = length(source) j = length(target) operations = [] while i > 0 or j > 0: if source and target elements match and diagonal predecessor is optimal: operations.append(MATCH) i -= 1 j -= 1 else if substitution predecessor is optimal: operations.append(SUBSTITUTE) i -= 1 j -= 1 else if deletion predecessor is optimal: operations.append(DELETE) i -= 1 else: operations.append(INSERT) j -= 1 reverse(operations)
The script is reversed at the end because backtracking proceeds from target state toward the source state.

sections.heading: The Optimal Edit Script May Not Be Unique
sections.evidence: The minimum numerical distance does not necessarily determine one unique script.
paragraphs: The minimum numerical distance does not necessarily determine one unique script.
Several predecessor states can satisfy:
D[i][j] = D[predecessor] + operation cost
with the same minimum total value.
Therefore:
unique distance ≠ necessarily unique optimal alignment
This matters when software reports individual substitutions, deletions, or insertions rather than only the final distance.

sections.heading: Tie-Breaking Changes the Reported Script
sections.evidence: When several optimal predecessors exist, an implementation can use a stable preference such as:
paragraphs: When several optimal predecessors exist, an implementation can use a stable preference such as:
match → substitution → deletion → insertion
to produce deterministic output.
This does not make the mathematical optimum unique. It simply selects one representative optimal path.
A system reporting edit statistics should document its cost model, alignment rules, and tie-breaking policy.

sections.heading: Edit Coordinates Must Be Defined
sections.evidence: Insertions and deletions shift later positions.
paragraphs: Insertions and deletions shift later positions.
abcdef ↓ delete b acdef
A later operation described as occurring at “position 4” can refer to:
the original source coordinates,
the current intermediate sequence,
the final target coordinates,
alignment coordinates.
APIs exposing edit scripts should define their coordinate system explicitly.

sections.heading: Weighted Edit Operations
sections.evidence: Standard Levenshtein distance assigns unit costs, but application-specific models can define:
paragraphs: Standard Levenshtein distance assigns unit costs, but application-specific models can define:
c_insert(a) c_delete(a) c_substitute(a,b)
For example, an OCR model could assign a lower substitution cost to character pairs that the recognizer frequently confuses.

Operation Illustrative Cost Possible Interpretation substitute(m,n) 0.4 Frequent recognition confusion substitute(q,z) 1.5 Less plausible confusion delete(space) 0.3 Frequent segmentation error insert(character) 1.0 Default insertion
The resulting algorithm minimizes total edit cost rather than simply counting operations.

sections.heading: Asymmetric Costs
sections.evidence: Edit costs can be directional:
paragraphs: Edit costs can be directional:
c_substitute(a,b) = 0.4 c_substitute(b,a) = 0.8
Such models can be useful when one sequence represents the output of an error-generating process relative to another.
But directional costs can produce:
d(x,y) ≠ d(y,x)
so the resulting function is no longer the ordinary symmetric Levenshtein metric.

sections.heading: Zero-Cost Transformations and Preprocessing
sections.evidence: Some applications deliberately treat selected differences as irrelevant.
paragraphs: Some applications deliberately treat selected differences as irrelevant.
One approach is to assign zero cost to a particular operation.
Another is to transform the text before computing edit distance:
raw text ↓ transformation T ↓ sequence representation ↓ edit distance
If:
x ≠ y but T(x) = T(y)
then:
ED(T(x), T(y)) = 0
This does not establish equality of the original strings. It establishes equality in the transformed comparison space.
See Text Normalization and Transliteration .

sections.heading: Transposition Is Not a Classical Levenshtein Operation
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
hte the
Two adjacent symbols have exchanged positions.
Classical Levenshtein distance contains only:
insertion deletion substitution
so an adjacent transposition is not one primitive Levenshtein edit.
Models that explicitly include transposition produce a different edit-distance model.
See Damerau-Levenshtein Distance .

sections.heading: The Operation Set Defines the Distance Model
sections.evidence: Allowed Operations Resulting Model Substitution only Related to Hamming distance on equal-length sequences Insertion + deletion Insert-delete distance related to longest common subsequence Insertion + deletion + substitution Standard Levenshtein distance Add adjacent transposition Damerau-style edit distance Symbol-dependent costs Weighted edit distance Gap-open + gap-extension costs Sequence-alignment models
paragraphs: Allowed Operations Resulting Model Substitution only Related to Hamming distance on equal-length sequences Insertion + deletion Insert-delete distance related to longest common subsequence Insertion + deletion + substitution Standard Levenshtein distance Add adjacent transposition Damerau-style edit distance Symbol-dependent costs Weighted edit distance Gap-open + gap-extension costs Sequence-alignment models
The phrase edit distance is therefore incomplete unless the sequence representation, operation set, and cost model are known.

sections.heading: Insertion-Deletion Distance and Longest Common Subsequence
sections.evidence: When substitution is not available as a primitive operation, transformation can be performed using deletions and insertions.
paragraphs: When substitution is not available as a primitive operation, transformation can be performed using deletions and insertions.
If L is a longest common subsequence of x and y , then under unit insertion and deletion costs:
d_insdel(x,y) = |x| + |y| - 2|L|
Symbols belonging to the common subsequence can remain unchanged. Other source elements are deleted, while missing target elements are inserted.

sections.heading: What Exactly Is One Edit Unit?
sections.evidence: In software, the word character is often ambiguous.
paragraphs: In software, the word character is often ambiguous.
One edit can act on:
bytes,
encoding code units,
Unicode code points,
extended grapheme clusters,
words or tokens,
phonemes,
DNA bases,
other application-defined sequence elements.
delete one byte ≠ delete one code point ≠ delete one grapheme cluster ≠ delete one word
The abstract edit operation is the same, but its application meaning changes with the underlying sequence representation.

sections.heading: Unicode Changes the Meaning of an Edit
sections.evidence: Consider the visible character:
paragraphs: Consider the visible character:
é
Unicode can represent it as:
or using a decomposed sequence:
A code-point-level edit model sees different sequence lengths in these two representations.
Likewise, one user-perceived emoji or decorated text unit can contain multiple Unicode code points.
Therefore:
Unicode code point ≠ necessarily one user-perceived character
See Unicode & Grapheme-Safe Levenshtein .

sections.heading: Normalization Can Change the Edit Script
sections.evidence: Canonically equivalent Unicode text can produce different edit operations when compared before normalization.
paragraphs: Canonically equivalent Unicode text can produce different edit operations when compared before normalization.
raw representation A vs raw representation B ↓ edit script 1
After canonical normalization:
NFC(A) vs NFC(B) ↓ edit script 2
the two strings can become identical or require fewer operations.
Therefore the edit script depends on the representation and transformation policy used before comparison.

sections.heading: Unicode Text Transformations and Edit Operations
sections.evidence: A Unicode transformation can intentionally produce a new valid sequence.
paragraphs: A Unicode transformation can intentionally produce a new valid sequence.
source Unicode text ↓ transformation T ↓ target Unicode text
Edit distance can then describe the minimum sequence changes connecting the source representation and the result.
source ↓ insert / delete / substitute ↓ result
The transformation and edit distance are separate operations:
transformation = produces the target representation edit distance = measures a minimum relationship between defined sequences
This distinction applies to normalization, transliteration, case transformations, and other Unicode mappings.
Continue with Unicode Text Transformations .

sections.heading: Character-Level Versus Token-Level Edits
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
the black cat the cat
At word level:
delete("black")
is one edit.
At character level, multiple characters and spacing must be removed.

Sequence Unit Meaning of One Deletion Code point Remove one Unicode code point Grapheme cluster Remove one user-perceived text unit Word Remove one token Phoneme Remove one phonetic unit DNA base Remove one nucleotide symbol

sections.heading: Edit Operations in Word Error Rate
sections.evidence: Automatic speech-recognition evaluation commonly applies insertion, deletion, and substitution to word sequences.
paragraphs: Automatic speech-recognition evaluation commonly applies insertion, deletion, and substitution to word sequences.
S = substitutions D = deletions I = insertions N = reference words WER = (S + D + I) / N
The edit operations resemble Levenshtein distance, but the sequence elements are words rather than characters and the final error statistic includes a task-specific normalization.
See Word Error Rate and ASR Evaluation .

sections.heading: Edit Operations in OCR Evaluation
sections.evidence: OCR systems can be evaluated through character-level or word-level insertions, deletions, and substitutions.
paragraphs: OCR systems can be evaluated through character-level or word-level insertions, deletions, and substitutions.
Separating error types can reveal behavior hidden by a single aggregate edit distance.
System Insertions Deletions Substitutions System A 10 8 82 System B 40 40 20
Two systems can therefore have the same total number of edit errors while producing very different error profiles.
See OCR Evaluation and Post-Correction .

sections.heading: Edit Operations in Biological Sequence Alignment
sections.evidence: Biological sequence analysis also uses insertion, deletion, and substitution concepts, but many alignment models use richer scoring systems.
paragraphs: Biological sequence analysis also uses insertion, deletion, and substitution concepts, but many alignment models use richer scoring systems.
A gap of length five can be modeled as:
one gap opening + four gap extensions
rather than five independent unit-cost deletions.
gap_cost(k) = gap_open + (k - 1) × gap_extend
This is a different model from standard Levenshtein distance.
See Sequence Alignment and Gap Models .

sections.heading: Edit Scripts as Explanations
sections.evidence: A scalar distance answers:
paragraphs: A scalar distance answers:
How much minimum editing separates the two sequences?
An edit script additionally answers:
Which permitted operations form one minimum-cost explanation of the difference?
This makes edit scripts useful for:
error analysis,
visual diff interfaces,
correction systems,
sequence alignment,
OCR analysis,
ASR diagnostics,
debugging.

sections.heading: An Optimal Edit Script Is Not a Causal History
sections.evidence: Suppose an optimal script contains:
paragraphs: Suppose an optimal script contains:
substitute a → e
This does not prove that a real-world process literally replaced an a with an e .
It means only that substitution belongs to one minimum-cost mathematical transformation under the selected sequence representation and cost model.
optimal edit script ≠ proven causal history
The actual difference may have originated from typing behavior, OCR, speech recognition, data conversion, text normalization, or another process.

sections.heading: The Conceptual Hierarchy
sections.evidence: source data ↓ optional transformation ↓ sequence representation ↓ allowed edit operations ↓ operation costs ↓ valid edit scripts ↓ minimum-cost script ↓ edit distance
paragraphs: source data ↓ optional transformation ↓ sequence representation ↓ allowed edit operations ↓ operation costs ↓ valid edit scripts ↓ minimum-cost script ↓ edit distance
Changing the transformation, sequence representation, permitted operations, or operation costs can change both the edit script and the final distance.

sections.heading: Key Distinctions
sections.evidence: Concept Meaning Edit operation One permitted sequence transformation step Match Zero-cost correspondence between equal sequence elements Edit script Ordered operations transforming source into target Valid script Any permitted script that reaches the target Optimal script A valid script with minimum total cost Edit distance Cost of an optimal script Alignment A positional representation of matches and edits Transformation A separate function that produces a new representation
paragraphs: Concept Meaning Edit operation One permitted sequence transformation step Match Zero-cost correspondence between equal sequence elements Edit script Ordered operations transforming source into target Valid script Any permitted script that reaches the target Optimal script A valid script with minimum total cost Edit distance Cost of an optimal script Alignment A positional representation of matches and edits Transformation A separate function that produces a new representation

sections.heading: Summary
sections.evidence: Insertion, deletion, and substitution are the elementary operations underlying standard Levenshtein distance.
paragraphs: Insertion, deletion, and substitution are the elementary operations underlying standard Levenshtein distance.
An edit script combines these operations into a complete transformation from source to target, while Levenshtein distance is defined by the cost of a minimum-cost valid script.
A minimum distance does not necessarily imply a unique alignment or edit script. Tie-breaking, coordinate systems, and representation choices matter whenever individual operations are interpreted.
Weighted costs, transpositions, gap models, and other extensions create different edit-distance models.

Unicode adds another essential requirement: one edit must be defined relative to a sequence representation. Bytes, code units, Unicode code points, grapheme clusters, and words are different edit units.
Define the representation, define the permitted operations, define their costs, then interpret the edit script.
